## Simple Random Sampling (SRS)



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# load needed packages

library(tidyverse)
library(maps)
```
:::



While you often don't get to have the full population as a sampling frame, we are going to walk through an example today to investigate the mathematical qualities of simple random sampling.

We are going to consider the population of countries included in the data from the World Bank put together in June 2019 by the authors of "Statistics: UnLocking the Power of Data." 

We are interested in estimating the average C02 emissions per-capita of a countries in the world.

3. In a previous class, we asked students to think of 10 countries that they believed were representative of the countries in the world (i.e., they resemble the collection of all countries of the world). Why is this not the best way to get a sample to estimate the average CO2 emissions? Do you thing the estimate would be biased, and in what direction?


:::{.version-solution}

*It is pretty difficult to think about what a "representative" sample of world countries would be unless you are an expert in Political Science or Geography... and even so. As you can see from the judgement samples that we did in all three sections of class this time around, we tended to think about countries that are LARGE on the map and that come up more often in US history and politics... As expected, this leads to a bias toward systematically overestimating C02 emissions.*

:::

4. Let's do simple random sampling instead. How many ways are there to select a sample $\mathcal{S}$ of size $n = 10$ from the population of 204 countries? Write out the formula you use and the output from R. (Hint: use the `choose()` function in R)

:::{.version-solution}

Total # of samples = $\binom{N}{n} = \binom{204}{10}  \approx  2.74926 \times 10^{16} = 27,492,600,000,000,000$ 

🫣 that's a lot of possible samples!

:::



::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# number of ways to select a sample of size 10
```
:::




::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# number of ways to select a sample of size 10

choose(204, 10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.74926e+16
```


:::
:::


5. Calculate the probability of selecting a sample $\mathcal{S}$ of size $n = 10$ using SRS. 

:::{.version-solution}
$P(\mathcal{S}) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{n}} = \frac{1}{2.74926 \times 10^{16}} \approx 3.64 \times 10^{-17}$ (very very small!)
:::


::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# probability of selecting a sample

1/choose(204, 10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.637343e-17
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# probability of selecting a sample
```

:::{.version-solution}

9. How different were your two sample estimates from the population mean? 

:::{.version-solution}
**Answers will vary: one of my random samples is a large over-estimate. But as we will see, the INDIVIDUAL samples don't matter -- what matters is the long-term behaviors of the estimates.**
:::

10. Now let's see what happens if we repeat this process many times (5,000 to be exact), taking a sample of 10 countries. I went ahead and did this for you. The plot below is a histogram of the sample mean C02 emissions. **Note** If you are reading this on the Quarto template, you will need to look back at the online version to see the figure.


:::{.version-instructions .version-student}
a. What is the shape of the sampling distribution? Is this what you expected? Explain.
b. Where is the sampling distribution centered? Why does this make sense?
c. Why is the center of this sampling distribution not exactly $\mu$?
:::

:::{.version-solution}
a. What is the shape of the sampling distribution? Is this what you expected? Explain. *The shape is more normal than the original sample distribution, but it is still somewhat skewed! This is expected since the sampling distribution of sample means tends to be normal, but if you have a very skewed distribution and small sample size, it will still be a bit skewed.*
b. Where is the sampling distribution centered? Why does this make sense? *The mean of the distribution is 5.01, which is very close to the population mean $\mu = 4.98$.*
c. Why is the center of this sampling distribution not exactly $\mu$? *This only represents an empirical distribution of 5,000 possible samples of countries -- not all $\binom{204}{10}$ possible samples! If we had a distribution wth ALL of them, the mean would be exactly $\mu$*
:::




::: {.cell version='["instructions","solution"]'}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
sample_mean_fun <- function(dat, size, var){
  
  dat |> 
    slice_sample(n = size) |> 
    summarize(mean_val = mean({{var}}, na.rm = T)) |> 
    pull(mean_val)
  
}

set.seed(30353)

sim <- map_dbl(.x = 1:5000,
               .f = ~sample_mean_fun(countries, size = 10, var = CO2))
```
